strengths: Reconstructing highly dynamic, transparent, and emissive phenomena like fire from only three sparse viewpoints is a challenging and valuable research direction.

The proposed hardware-software co-design is highly practical. Using a low-cost microcontroller-based visual synchronization pattern and explicitly modeling the rolling-shutter effects of CMOS sensors enables high-quality, high-speed capture with affordable consumer-grade hardware.

The initialization and optimization strategy is well-designed, fusing multi-view stereo, monocular depth priors, and back-projected 3D optical flow to reliably constrain both the static background and the highly under-constrained dynamic flame region.
The paper introduces a high-quality, real-world dataset of 17 dynamic fire sequences spanning different fuel types (wood, gasoline, propane, cardboard, paper) captured at 400Hz.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, including comprehensive ablation studies, show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting baselines.
weaknesses: The core representation for the dynamic Gaussians relies directly on FreeTimeGS [88], meaning the algorithmic novelty regarding the dynamic scene representation itself is somewhat limited.

The decoupling of the static background and dynamic fire assumes minimal background-foreground interaction. Since fire is highly emissive, it casts dynamic light and reflections on the static background, which is not explicitly modeled and might lead to baked-in illumination artifacts.

The evaluation of depth reconstruction accuracy (RMSE_depth in Tab. 1) relies on a monocular depth estimation model (DepthAnythingV2) as a pseudo-ground-truth, which itself may not be fully accurate or consistent for transparent and emissive flames.

strengths: Addresses a highly challenging and important problem: reconstructing the high-frequency, non-rigid, and semi-transparent geometry of dynamic flames from extremely sparse views (only three cameras).

Presents a complete, clever, and practical hardware-software co-design. Specifically, exploiting the CMOS rolling shutter effect with a microcontroller-driven LED strip pattern to achieve sub-frame microsecond-level synchronization (15 µs precision) is a very creative and cost-effective engineering solution.

Provides a robust initialization scheme by projecting dense 2D optical flows into a 3D voxel grid to initialize FreeTimeGS, which significantly mitigates the highly under-constrained optimization under sparse viewpoints.

Introduces a new high-frequency real-world dataset of diverse fire sequences (17 videos of different fuel types captured at 400 Hz), which will be released publicly and should be highly valuable for the community.
Shows significant quantitative and qualitative improvements over standard 4D Gaussian Splatting baselines, demonstrating visually realistic renderings and geometrically plausible shapes.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty of the core 3D representation is somewhat limited, as it heavily builds on existing building blocks like 3DGS, FreeTimeGS, and MEMFOF. The paper is primarily an Applied/Systems contribution.

The depth evaluation metric (RMSE_depth) relies on comparing the rendered depth against aligned monocular depth predictions (DepthAnythingV2). Since monocular depth models are not trained on transparent, emissive flames and often perform poorly or inconsistently in such regions, using them as a pseudo-ground truth may introduce bias.

The performance of the dynamic initialization heavily depends on the quality of 2D optical flow (MEMFOF). Dynamic flames exhibit complex physical phenomena like transparency, refraction, and rapid intensity changes, which violate brightness constancy. A deeper discussion or ablation on how optical flow errors affect the final 3D reconstruction would strengthen the work.
The method requires separating the static background from the dynamic foreground, which limits applicability to setups with moving cameras or dynamic backgrounds.

strengths: Addresses a highly challenging and practical problem: reconstructing high-frequency, volumetric, and semi-transparent fire dynamics from extremely sparse (only three) views.

Proposes a well-designed pipeline that decouples static background and dynamic flame reconstruction, using monocular and stereo depth fusion for the background and a 3D fused flow field initialization for the flame.

Presents a clever hardware-software co-design: utilizing a low-cost LED-based synchronization pattern and exploiting rolling shutter effects to achieve microsecond-level synchronization using consumer-grade cameras (GoPros at 400Hz).
Introduces a new real-world high-frame-rate dataset with 17 diverse fire scenarios (different fuels and backgrounds), which will be released to the community.

Provides a thorough evaluation, with robust quantitative and qualitative improvements over standard 4D Gaussian Splatting baselines, supported by detailed per-scene results and ablation studies in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The motion representation (linear velocity with Gaussian lifetimes based on FreeTimeGS) is relatively simple and may fail to capture highly turbulent, non-linear fluid dynamics of flames over longer intervals, leading to temporal oversmoothing.

Reliance on 2D dense optical flow (MEMFOF) to initialize the 3D flow field makes the method sensitive to flow errors. Emissive variations, rapid appearance changes, and low-texture regions in flames can cause inaccurate flow predictions that propagate into the 3D reconstruction.

The assumption that the static background and the dynamic flame can be cleanly decoupled ignores complex physical interactions, such as thick smoke occluding the background or strong dynamic illumination and reflections cast by the fire onto the static scene.

The synchronization pattern is physically intrusive, meaning the LED board must be visible in the camera views during capture. This limits the setup to controlled environments and prevents reconstruction of spontaneous, real-world fires 'in the wild'.

strengths: Addresses an exceptionally challenging and under-explored task: sparse-view (three-camera) 3D reconstruction of dynamic, semi-transparent, and emissive flames.
Proposes a well-designed pipeline that decouples static background and dynamic fire, combining stereo-monocular depth fusion with a novel flow-based initialization for transient Gaussians.
Deploys an innovative and low-cost rolling-shutter visual synchronization setup utilizing an ESP32 and LEDs, achieving microsecond-level temporal alignment with consumer hardware.
Introduces both a high-speed real-world dataset (captured at 400 Hz across 17 diverse scenarios) and synthetic fire simulations containing ground-truth velocity fields.
Defines a novel, density-weighted volumetric evaluation protocol (DVE) to quantify velocity field accuracy, providing a rigorous and physically meaningful comparison against baselines.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting approaches.
weaknesses: The linear velocity model may struggle with highly turbulent or vortical motion, which can cause temporal blurring or require artificially small lifespans for the Gaussians.
The pipeline relies heavily on the quality of the 2D optical flow (MEMFOF); any failures in flow estimation on saturated or textureless flame regions can directly degrade the 3D flow initialization.

The static-dynamic separation assumes minimal background-foreground interaction. In real scenarios, strong illumination changes on the background caused by the fluctuating flames might violate this assumption, leading to artifacts.
The physical LED synchronization board must be visible in the camera views, which restricts the setup to controlled environments and prevents truly casual or in-the-wild capture.

strengths: Addresses the highly challenging and under-explored task of sparse-view (3-camera) reconstruction of transient, non-rigid, and emissive volumetric phenomena (fire), which is a known failure case for existing dynamic 3DGS methods.

Combines background/foreground separation, dense multi-view stereo, monocular depth priors, and 3D flow field initialization from projected 2D optical flow to reliably bootstrap the under-constrained dynamic optimization.

Proposes a clever and low-cost sub-frame synchronization scheme using an ESP32 microcontroller and LED strips (leveraging CMOS rolling shutter effects) to achieve 15-microsecond temporal precision on consumer cameras.

Establishes a rigorous evaluation protocol (Density-weighted Volumetric Evaluation - DVE) using physical simulation (Mantaflow/Blender) and provides a diverse real-world high-speed fire dataset across multiple fuel types.
weaknesses: The constant linear velocity and short lifespan model relies on very high-speed cameras (400 Hz). The paper does not thoroughly analyze or demonstrate performance under standard consumer video frame rates (e.g., 30 or 60 fps) where temporal displacement is much larger and non-linear.

The initialization is heavily dependent on 2D optical flow (MEMFOF) and monocular depth estimators. If the flame has chaotic textureless regions or is heavily obscured by smoke, these priors can fail and propagate errors into the 3D velocity field.

The sub-frame synchronization scheme requires the LED strips to be visible to all cameras, which restricts camera placement and field of view, making it less practical for larger or more unstructured capture environments.

The offline decoupling of static background and dynamic flame assumes a static background with minimal interaction. This might fail in situations where the fire deforms the background (e.g., burning/collapsing wood) or creates significant dynamic lighting/shadow effects on the background.

strengths: Tackles a highly challenging and underexplored problem: reconstructing transient, emissive, and non-rigid volumetric phenomena (fire/flames) from extremely sparse viewpoints (only three views).

Presents a well-motivated and technically sound method that decomposes the scene into static and dynamic parts, using 3D flow fields back-projected from 2D optical flows to initialize transient Gaussians.

Introduces a clever, low-cost visual synchronization setup exploiting the rolling shutter effect of commodity CMOS cameras, achieving microsecond-level synchronization without expensive hardware triggers.

Provides a comprehensive evaluation protocol (DVE) for verifying reconstructed velocity fields against physical simulation ground truth, alongside a high-quality real-world dataset of 17 fire sequences captured at 400 Hz.
The paper is very well-written, clearly illustrated, and includes extensive quantitative and qualitative results, ablation studies, and detailed implementation specs in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The pipeline heavily depends on multiple pre-existing models (COLMAP, DepthAnythingV2, and MEMFOF). Performance might degrade significantly if these upstream models produce noisy outputs in challenging lighting or smoky conditions.

The constant-velocity motion model with a short lifetime is a simplified representation of fluid/combustion dynamics. Under highly turbulent conditions, it may lead to temporal oversmoothing or blurring.

While synthetic validation is used to evaluate the 3D velocity field, there is no direct geometric ground-truth evaluation for the real-world reconstructions (e.g., via tomography or structured light), which is an inherent limitation of the topic but worth noting.
